# ledger_client

LedgerClient - the Ruby gem for the Ledger Service

The app records entries with the ledger service through this API. Every request has a service token in the Authorization header, and the ledger rejects a token it did not issue with 401. Amounts are integers in the smallest unit of the account's currency, so 1050 in a USD account is ten dollars and fifty cents. An entry cannot change once the ledger accepts it, and a correction is a second entry with the opposite sign that gives the first entry's id in its reference field. The ledger keeps entries in the order it accepted them, and an account's balance is the sum of its entries at the moment of the read, so two reads a second apart can differ while entries are arriving. Listing accounts returns every account the token can see, newest first, and the list is not paginated, because a token sees at most a few hundred accounts. Reading one account returns 404 when the id is unknown or belongs to an account the token cannot see, so a caller cannot tell the two apart. Creating an entry returns 201 with the stored entry, including the id the ledger assigned and the time it was accepted. It returns 422 when the amount is zero or not an integer, when the account is closed, or when the reference gives an entry in another account. A request with the same Idempotency-Key header as an earlier one within twenty-four hours returns the earlier response instead of creating a second entry, which makes a retry after a timeout safe. The ledger returns 429 when one token sends more than fifty requests a second, with a Retry-After header in seconds, and 503 during its weekly maintenance window early on Sunday mornings UTC, also with Retry-After. Clients should treat 503 and 429 the same way and retry after the given delay. Every response has an X-Request-Id header, which the ledger team asks callers to log and quote when they report a problem. Field names are snake_case throughout, timestamps are RFC 3339 strings in UTC, and ids are opaque strings that callers must not parse. New optional fields may appear in responses at any time without a version change, so callers should ignore fields they do not know.
